title: The Amman Message
hook: in 2004 hundreds of scholars recognized the eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zahiris, and your line: the plain sense. When you reread what someone actually said, was it different from what you first heard? Day one thousand two hundred six.

One word can end a conversation for good. In Arabic it's takfir: declaring another Muslim an unbeliever. Said by the wrong person at the wrong time, it doesn't just insult. It can put a target on someone's back. Now, Amman, the capital of Jordan, and a different kind of sentence. Scholars from Sunni, Shia and Ibadi schools, people who disagree about hands in prayer, about the moon, about who should lead, put their names to a list of schools and said: these are all Muslims. Today, the Amman Message.
screen: `TAKFIR: CALLING A MUSLIM AN UNBELIEVER.` → `A ROOM IN AMMAN.` → `THESE ARE ALL MUSLIMS.`

segments.voice: First, the message. In 2004, the Amman Message was issued in Jordan, under King Abdullah the Second, as a statement of what Islam is and is not. Then came a question put to senior scholars of different schools, and their answers became three points. Next, the first point: the names. Whoever follows one of the four Sunni schools, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i or Hanbali, or the Ja'fari school, or the Zaydi, or the Ibadi, or the Zahiri, is a Muslim. Count them: eight. The schools of these last few days are there by name. Then, the second point: the word from the hook. It is not permitted, the Message says, to declare the followers of these schools unbelievers. Takfir is closed off between them. Hundreds of scholars endorsed those points, by the Message's own record. Last, the third point: who may speak. A fatwa, a formal legal opinion, belongs to people qualified in a school's method, and no one may issue one outside that method. That's a guard against anyone with a microphone deciding who's in and who's out. Under all three sits a Qur'an verse the schools share. In Pickthall's words: "hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The Message doesn't erase difference. The schools still pray with different hands and argue in their books. What it says is that the arguing happens inside one family. Eight schools, one ummah, one community of believers.
screen: `AMMAN, JORDAN: A MESSAGE.` · `EIGHT SCHOOLS, NAMED.` · `NO TAKFIR BETWEEN THEM.` · `ONLY THE QUALIFIED GIVE FATWAS.`

segments.voice: The practice: read about it, starting with its list. Say the eight names slowly, one per breath. Hanafi. Maliki. Shafi'i. Hanbali. Ja'fari. Zaydi. Ibadi. Zahiri. Notice which ones you know a little now, and which still feel like strangers. Then think of one person whose practice differs from yours, in any faith or none, and hold the thought: we disagree, and we're still neighbors. If you pray, you can pray for unity among those who pray. Later today, find the text of the Message itself and read its three points. The bell holds the time.
The Amman Message. Issued in Jordan; scholars named eight schools of law, and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers. Today's word.

Your line: eight schools, one ummah. That closes our visit to the other houses. Next, how the schools actually differ, starting with something you can see: the hands. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: The Amman Message and its three points recognize eight schools of law, the four Sunni schools with the Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ibadi and Zahiri, forbid declaring their followers unbelievers, and limit fatwas to those qualified in a school's method.

original.note: Arabic: takfir, declaring someone an unbeliever, which the Amman Message forbids between the eight schools.

what it means: the Amman Message names eight schools as Muslim and closes off takfir between them.
what a scholar hears: the three points of Amman, the question put to senior scholars, and the guard on who may issue a fatwa.

notes: Editor: hook no longer stages scholars reading out a list in one room (the three points came through rulings and later endorsements); practice opener reworded.
Date (2004) and issue under King Abdullah II taken from the Amman Message's own record; confirm. The three points were issued after a 2005 conference; the script avoids that date.
'Hundreds of scholars endorsed' from the outline and the Message's own record; confirm.
Three points as summarized (eight schools named, no takfir, fatwa conditions): confirm wording. The points also recognize Ash'ari theology, Sufism and true Salafi thought; omitted for focus.
The hook says scholars from Sunni, Shia and Ibadi schools were involved: confirm.
Carry closes the part 'The Ja'fari school and other traditions' (1198–1206) and points to 'How the schools differ' (1207–1214).
